## {#data-never-ready data-menu-title="Data Is Never Ready"}

[Data is rarely in the format we need]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The data we get to work with are **rarely, if ever, in the format we 
need** to do our analyses.

It's often the case that:

- One package requires data in one format
- Another package requires it in a different format
- The shape of the data doesn't match our research question

To be **efficient analysts**, we need good tools for reformatting data.
:::

---

## {#dplyr-tidyr data-menu-title="dplyr and tidyr"}

[Enter `dplyr` and `tidyr`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The `dplyr` and `tidyr` R packages provide a **fairly complete and 
extremely powerful** set of functions for reformatting data quickly.

Learning these tools well will greatly **increase your efficiency** as 
an analyst.
:::

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**`dplyr`** — for transforming rows and columns

**`tidyr`** — for reshaping the structure of data frames
:::

---

## {#motivating-ex1 data-menu-title="Motivating Example 1"}

[Motivating Example 1: Summarizing]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Suppose you have salmon length data and want to calculate the **average 
length per year**.
:::

:::{.smaller}
| year | length_cm |
|------|-----------|
| 1990 | 5.6773318 |
| 1991 | 3.081224 |
| 1991 | 4.526969 |
| 1992 | 4.381523 |
| 1992 | 5.597777 |
| 1992 | 4..900052|
:::

. . .

:::{.body-text}
Before writing code — **what are the steps?** (think pseudocode)
:::

---

## {#motivating-ex1-code data-menu-title="Example 1 Code"}

[Motivating Example 1: The Code]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The `dplyr` package lets us express those steps as a **readable 
pipeline**:
:::

```r
length_data %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  summarize(mean_length_cm = mean(length_cm))
```

:::{.body-text}
Read it as: *"Take the data, **then** group by year, **then** 
summarize by calculating mean length."*
:::

---

## {#motivating-ex2 data-menu-title="Motivating Example 2"}

[Motivating Example 2: Reshaping]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Consider this **wide format** table — a common data entry format:
:::

:::{.smaller}
| site   | 1990 | 1991 | … | 1993 |
|--------|------|------|---|------|
| gold   | 100  | 118  | … | 112  |
| lake   | 100  | 118  | … | 112  |
| …    |  …   |  … | … | …   |
| dredge | 100  | 118  | … | 112  |
:::

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**Problem:** How would you fit a model with year as a predictor?

`lm(length ~ year)` won't work — `year` isn't a column, it's a set of 
column names.
:::

---

## {#motivating-ex2-code data-menu-title="Example 2 Code"}

[Motivating Example 2: The Code]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`tidyr` lets us reshape from wide to long:
:::

```r
site_data %>% 
  pivot_longer(-site, 
               names_to = "year", 
               values_to = "length")
```

:::{.smaller}
| site   | year | length |
|--------|------|--------|
| gold   | 1990 | 101    |
| lake   | 1990 | 104    |
| dredge | 1990 | 144    |
| …      | …    | …      |
| dredge | 1993 | 145    |
:::

---

## {#function-tables data-menu-title="Function Reference"}

[Key Functions We'll Use]{.slide-title}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**`dplyr` functions**

| Function | What it does |
|----------|-------------|
| `select()` | Keep or drop columns |
| `filter()` | Keep rows by condition |
| `mutate()` | Create or change columns |
| `rename()` | Rename a column |
| `group_by()` | Group data |
| `summarize()` | Summarize each group |
| `arrange()` | Sort rows |
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**`tidyr` functions**

| Function | What it does |
|----------|-------------|
| `pivot_longer()` | Wide → long |
| `pivot_wider()` | Long → wide |
| `separate()` | Split one column into many |
| `unite()` | Combine columns into one |
:::
:::

## {#dataset-intro data-menu-title="The Dataset"}

[Our Dataset: Alaska Salmon Catches]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
We'll use a tidied version of commercial catch data from the **Alaska 
Department of Fish & Game, 1878–1997**.

Available from the [KNB Data Repository](https://knb.ecoinformatics.org/#view/df35b.304.2).
:::

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)

catch_original <- read_csv(
  "https://knb.ecoinformatics.org/knb/d1/mn/v2/object/df35b.302.1"
)
```

---

## {#package-masking data-menu-title="A Note on Package Masking"}

[A Note on Package Masking]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
When you load `dplyr`, you'll see this message:
:::

```
Attaching package: 'dplyr'
The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
    filter, lag
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
This means `dplyr`'s `filter()` now takes precedence over `stats`'s 
`filter()`.

To be explicit about which package's function you want, use:

`package_name::function_name()`

Example: `stats::filter()` vs `dplyr::filter()`
:::

---

## {#data-exploration data-menu-title="Data Exploration"}

[Step 1: Explore Before You Transform]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Before wrangling, always **familiarize yourself with the data**.
:::

```r
## Column names
colnames(catch_original)

## First 6 rows
head(catch_original)

## Summary of each column
summary(catch_original)

## Unique values in a column
unique(catch_original$Region)

## Open in viewer (use in console)
View(catch_original)
```

---

## {#explore-why data-menu-title="Why Explore First"}

[Why Explore First?]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Data exploration helps you:

- Confirm the data was **read in correctly**
- Identify **unexpected data types** (numeric stored as character?)
- Spot **missing values** or obvious errors
- Understand the **structure** before deciding how to reshape

Think of it as reading a paper's methods section before jumping to 
the results — context matters.
:::

---

## {#pipe-intro data-menu-title="The Pipe Operator"}

[The Pipe Operator `%>%`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The pipe `%>%` takes the **output** of one step and passes it as the 
**input** to the next.
:::

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**Without the pipe:**
:::

```r
df_filtered <- filter(df, ...)
df_selected <- select(df_filtered, ...)
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**With the pipe:**
:::

```r
df_cleaned <- df %>% 
    filter(...) %>%
    select(...)
```

---

## {#pipe-reading data-menu-title="Reading the Pipe"}

[Reading Code with the Pipe]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Think of `<-` as **"gets"** and `%>%` as **"then"**.
:::

```r
df_cleaned <- df %>% 
    filter(...) %>%
    select(...)
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
> *"The cleaned data frame **gets** the original data, **then** a 
> filter, **then** a select."*

Each step in the pipeline is an **analytical decision**. 
The code reads like a narrative of your reasoning.
:::

---

## {#pipe-benefits data-menu-title="Pipe Benefits and Tradeoffs"}

[Benefits and Tradeoffs of Pipes]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
**Benefits:**

- No need to track or overwrite intermediate data frames
- Code reads sequentially — easier to follow the logic
- Easy to add or remove steps

**Tradeoffs:**

- Many chained steps can be harder to debug
- Harder to inspect intermediate results

Strike a balance: **chain related steps**, but **save intermediate 
objects** when they're meaningful checkpoints.
:::

---

## {#pipe-shortcut data-menu-title="Pipe Shortcut"}

[Keyboard Shortcut for `%>%`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text .center-text}
RStudio has a built-in shortcut for the pipe:

**Windows:** `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `M`

**Mac:** `Cmd` + `Shift` + `M`
:::

. . .

:::{.body-text}
You'll use this constantly. Worth memorizing now.
:::
